summary: This experimental document gives definitions, originally in RFC 1495 and RFC 1341, for carrying ODA (Office Document Architecture) in MIME and translating it to its X.400 representation.

plainLanguage.summary: Packing an office document for mail in a way two mail systems understand.

questions: how to send oda documents in email
subtitle: Carries office documents in email using a standard format

tldr.problem: Office documents created with Office Document Architecture (ODA) need a standard way to travel in email systems.
tldr.mechanism: Defines the MIME content-type application/oda with parameters for document class and application profile, allowing conversion between ODA (used in X.400 mail) and MIME (used in Internet email).
tldr.outcome: Mail gateways can reliably translate office documents between X.400 and MIME email systems.

today: RFC 2161 is an Experimental document defining ODA in MIME. The X.400 email system is largely historical; modern deployments use MIME-based Internet email directly.

sections.title: Office Documents in Email
sections.content: The Office Document Architecture (ODA) is an international standard for formatting documents. X.400 is an older email system that understands ODA documents natively. Internet email uses MIME for attachments. When email travels between X.400 and Internet systems, documents need translation. This document specifies how to represent ODA documents in MIME so that mail gateways can reliably carry them between systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Two old email systems need to understand office documents. One knows ODA, the other knows MIME. This explains how to translate between them.

sections.title: The MIME Content-Type
sections.content: ODA documents are sent as MIME type application/oda. Two required parameters describe the document: profile (such as Q112 for a common profile) and class (one of formatted, processable, or formatted-processable). For example: Content-Type: application/oda; profile=Q112; class=formatted. The document body is encoded using Base64 content-transfer-encoding. When no parameters are provided, defaults of Q112 profile and formatted-processable class are used.
sections.plainLanguage: The email says "this is an ODA document" and tells what kind it is. The document data is then encoded as text for email.

sections.title: Translation Between Systems
sections.content: Mail gateways map the MIME parameters to X.400 body part parameters and back. The gateway may optionally try to read profile and class information from inside the document itself, though this is not required. When translating from X.400 to MIME, the gateway extracts the document application profile and architecture class from the X.400 ODA body part. When translating from MIME to X.400, the gateway reads the parameters from the Content-Type header and sets the X.400 ODA body part parameters accordingly.
sections.plainLanguage: When documents cross between the two email systems, gateways read the labels, change them to the other system's format, and send the document on its way.

references.text: Freed, N., and N. Borenstein, "Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) Part One: Format of Internet Message Bodies", RFC 2045, November 1996.
